You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the failing test does:
  - SparseRealVectorTest.testEbeDivideMixedTypes calls doTestEbeBinaryOperation(BinaryOperation.DIV, true).
  - The helper builds two vectors v1 and v2 from all pairwise combinations of a values array. Because getPreferredEntryValue() returns 0, the values set includes 0 and 1/x where x = 0, i.e., Infinity. For division, this setup also creates cases like 0/0 (which should be NaN), 0/Infinity (0), and other finite divisions.
  - v1 is created as an OpenMapRealVector, and v2 is created as an “alien” RealVector implementation (dense array-backed), hence “mixed types”.
  - The expected result is computed element-wise as data1[i] / data2[i] using plain double arithmetic; the test asserts exact equality.

- Where it goes wrong:
  - OpenMapRealVector.ebeDivide(RealVector v) currently:
    - Creates the result as a copy of “this”: OpenMapRealVector res = new OpenMapRealVector(this).
    - Iterates only over non-zero entries of “this” (entries.iterator()) and sets res[i] = this[i] / v[i] for those indices.
    - Returns res without touching indices where this[i] == 0.
    - Although the method comment explicitly states “it is not sufficient to loop through non zero entries of this only” because 0/0 should be NaN (not 0), the code does exactly that: it only updates non-zero entries and leaves zeros unchanged.

- Consequence in the test:
  - For indices where this[i] == 0 and v[i] == 0, the mathematically correct result is NaN, but the implementation leaves res[i] at 0 (carried over from the copy), causing assertion failures.
  - Similarly, for indices where this[i] == 0 and v[i] is NaN, the correct result is NaN, but the implementation still leaves 0. For 0/Infinity the correct result is 0, which would pass by coincidence; however, 0/0 and 0/NaN will fail.

- Related issue for multiplication:
  - OpenMapRealVector.ebeMultiply(RealVector v) has the same structural problem: it only processes non-zero entries of “this”. For indices where this[i] == 0 and v[i] is Infinity or NaN, the correct result is NaN; but the code leaves those entries as 0. The method even contains a comment acknowledging these special cases but then returns without handling them.

- Root cause:
  - Both ebeDivide and ebeMultiply in OpenMapRealVector assume that operations can be restricted to non-zero entries of “this”. This assumption breaks when IEEE-754 special values are involved (0/0, 0/NaN, 0*Infinity, 0*NaN), leading to incorrect results (0 instead of NaN) for mixed-type operations and, in general, any case where the counterpart vector has zeros or non-finite values opposite zeros in “this”.

- Why this surfaces in the mixed-types test:
  - The test intentionally uses an OpenMapRealVector for the left-hand side and a different RealVector implementation for the right-hand side. The buggy OpenMapRealVector.ebeDivide path is used, triggering the bug on entries where the left-hand vector has zeros.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
